vignette: The fever breaks on a Tuesday. Four days earlier, Clara collapses behind the pass of the bistro where she works as a line cook. A ruptured ulcer, the trauma team explains later, plunges her into septic shock. She spends seventy-two hours in a drug-induced sleep while her staff rotates to keep the dinner service running. When she finally opens her eyes in the ICU, the first thing she notices is the rhythmic hiss of the ventilator. She counts the breaths automatically, her pulse racing to match the machine’s metronome. Now, months later and back in her own bed, that counting continues. At forty-three, she expects her body to behave like one. Sleep fractures into short, sharp intervals, shattered by the sudden certainty that her chest will not rise on its own. She lies perfectly still, afraid that any movement will trigger the same collapse. Her partner, Mateo, leaves jars of broth on the counter and leaves the television on low. She turns the volume down. The sight of clear liquid makes her throat tighten. She tells herself she is rebuilding, but her nervous system keeps a separate ledger. She returns to the kitchen after six weeks, drawn by the familiar geometry of stainless steel and the predictable weight of a Friday night service. The knives are still hers. The tickets still spit from the printer like machine gun fire. But now, every sizzle of rendered fat sounds like the flatline that nearly took her. She stands over the sauté pan with her shoulders locked, scanning the exhaust hood for smoke that isn’t there. When the sous chef calls a countdown—ten, nine, eight—her stomach drops. She finishes the plate with mechanical precision, but her hands are cold. She wipes them on her apron, over and over, until the cotton frays. Mateo notices the way she flinches when the walk-in cooler door slams shut. He asks if she wants to transition to prep work, where the mornings are quieter. She shakes her head. The kitchen is where she belongs, she says, even as the heat from the oven presses against her face like a physical weight. At night, she lies awake while Mateo sleeps beside her. Her mind replays the ICU monitors, the nurses speaking in hushed tones about pressors and lactate. She stops drinking red wine. She avoids restaurants with dim lighting. She tells herself she is fine, that the body remembers what it endured, but her jaw stays clenched from morning to night. Tonight, during the lull between the appetizer rush and the main course, she leans against the prep table. Her phone buzzes in her pocket—an appointment reminder, another marker of what almost happened. She doesn’t look at it. Instead, she focuses on the condensation on a glass of ice water, watching the droplets merge and fall. The pass is quiet for three seconds. In that silence, she feels entirely alone in the room, even though the kitchen is full of life. She straightens her chef’s coat, picks up a pair of tongs, and calls for the next course. Her voice is steady. Her hands are steady. She waits for the other shoe to drop, as it always does.
